newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil on tenterhooks over CVRD sale.
newsitem.headline: Brazil on tenterhooks over CVRD sale.

text.p: Michael Christie
Brazil's government, in a last-ditch attempt to keep Latin America's largest privatisation on track for Tuesday, lodged an appeal with a high court to battle an avalanche of lawsuits.

Earlier, about 2,000 leftist protesters turned downtown Rio de Janeiro into a battle ground when they clashed with riot police near the stock exchange where mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) was due to go on the auction block.
"Our aim is to hold the auction today," said Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros, head of the National Development Bank, which runs the government's privatisation programme.

Forty-five percent of voting shares of the world's largest iron ore exporter had been due to go under the hammer Tuesday morning but opponents flooded courts across the country with 110 lawsuits, delaying the sale.
Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said 19 injunctions were granted, and a small army of government lawyers flown around in hired jets had managed to have 16 of the injunction overturned.

In the evening, the government decided to resort to the Superior Court of Justice in Brasilia, arguing that a "conflict of interpretation" among the lower courts meant all lawsuits should be refered to a single higher tribunal.
The government said it had until 11:30 p.m. local time (0230 GMT) to win its case for the auction to take place Tuesday.
The privatisation of CVRD, the world's largest iron ore exporter, should raise at least $5 billion once completed and would be the biggest Latin American state sell-off ever.

The sale has attracted considerable controversy, with opponents ranging from former Presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco to the country's Catholic bishops accusing the government of selling the country out to foreigners for a pittance.
The flurry of lawsuits against the sale, a favourite tactic of privatisation foes, came as no surprise.
Nevertheless it seemed to have overwhelmed Brasilia.
Development bank chief Mendonca de Barros lashed out at the "illegitimate use and abuse of the legal system" by a "ferocious and hysterical opposition".

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said he was confident the Superior Court of Justice decision would go Brasilia's way but an aide to the minister conceded that the chance of total success was still "remote".
The legal battle was mirrored outside the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange where hundreds of demonstrators trying to break through a security cordon fought with police, throwing rocks and cans.
Police retreating towards the exchange fired stun grenades and tear gas into the crowds and called in water cannons.
Authorities said about 29 people were injured before the violence died down at around midday.
CVRD enjoys a rare public sector reputation for efficiency. It also owns the world's largest iron ore deposits with its Carajas mine in the Amazon thought to hold 18 billion metric tons.
Two multinational consortia were in the bidding.
One was being led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN and the other by local pulp, cement and metal concern Votorantim and Anglo American Corp. of South Africa Ltd.
